When a material is placed in an external magnetic field, its response depends on its magnetic properties. 

1. Paramagnetic Substances: A small magnetization occurs in the direction of the external field. Magnetic susceptibility \chi is a small but positive quantity (\chi $\approx$ 10^{-3} \text{ to } 10^{-5}). The relative permeability $\mu$_r = 1 + \chi is slightly more than 1. These substances are weakly attracted by a magnet. When a rod of paramagnetic material is suspended in a magnetic field, it aligns itself parallel to the field.

2. Ferromagnetic Substances: A large magnetization occurs in the direction of the field. The magnetic susceptibility is very large and positive (on the order of several thousands), and the relative permeability $\mu$_r is also on the order of thousands. These substances are strongly attracted by a magnet and normally exist only in the solid state. Like paramagnetic materials, a suspended ferromagnetic rod aligns parallel to the field.

3. Diamagnetic Substances: A small magnetization occurs in a direction opposite to the external field. The magnetic susceptibility \chi is small and negative. Consequently, the relative permeability $\mu$_r = 1 + \chi is slightly less than 1. These substances are weakly repelled by a magnet. When a rod of diamagnetic material is suspended in a magnetic field, it aligns itself perpendicular to the field.

Paramagnetism and diamagnetism can be found in solids, liquids, or gases, whereas ferromagnetism is typically restricted to the solid state.

[Figure: PART1: The diagram features three horizontal rectangular blocks labeled Ferromagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Diamagnetic, each placed in a field of horizontal lines with arrows pointing right. For the Ferromagnetic block, lines from a wide area converge sharply to crowd inside the rectangle, while the Paramagnetic block shows a much gentler inward curving of lines. In the Diamagnetic illustration, the field lines bend outward around the block, resulting in fewer lines passing through the material compared to the surrounding space.

PART2: This diagram clarifies the concept of magnetic permeability by visually demonstrating how different materials either concentrate or expel magnetic flux. It makes the abstract difference between "slightly more than one" and "thousands" for relative permeability concrete by showing the varying intensity of field line crowding. Seeing these patterns prevents the common mistake of assuming all materials that are attracted to magnets behave with the same intensity or failing to realize that diamagnetic materials actively push field lines away.]

With this symmetry, the magnetic field must be tangent to and constant in magnitude along any circular path centered on OO’. This allows us to write for each of the paths $D_{1} , D_{2} ,$ and $D_{3}$ shown in part (d) of the figure,

Ampère’s law relates this integral to the net current passing through any surface bounded by the path of integration. For a path that is external to the toroid, either no current passes through the enclosing surface (path $D_{1}$ ), or the current passing through the surface in one direction is exactly balanced by the current passing through it in the opposite direction $( \text{path} \,D_{3} ) .$ In either case, there is no net current passing through the surface, so

$\oint B ( 2 \pi r ) = 0$

and

$B = 0 \,(outside the toroid) .$

The turns of a toroid form a helix, rather than circular loops. As a result, there is a small field external to the coil; however, the derivation above holds if the coils were circular.

For a circular path within the toroid (path $D_{2}$ ), the current in the wire cuts the surface N times, resulting in a net current NI through the surface. We now find with Ampère’s law,

$B ( 2 \pi r ) = \mu_{0} N I$

and

$B = \frac{\mu_{0} N I}{2 \pi r} \,(within the toroid) .$

The magnetic field is directed in the counterclockwise direction for the windings shown. When the current in the coils is reversed, the direction of the magnetic field also reverses.

Strategy

The time period can be found from considering the equation $V_{C} ( t ) = \epsilon ( 1 - e^{- t / \tau} ) ,$ where $\tau = ( R + r ) C .$

Solution

The neon lamp flashes when the voltage across the capacitor reaches 80 V. The RC time constant is equal to $\tau = ( R + r ) C = ( 101 \,\Omega ) ( 50 \,\times \,10^{-3} \text{F} ) = 5.05 \,\text{s} .$ We can solve the voltage equation for the time it takes the capacitor to reach 80 V:

$\begin{matrix}V_{C} ( t ) & = & \epsilon ( 1 - e^{- t / \tau} ) , \\ e^{- t / \tau} & = & 1 - \frac{V_{C} ( t )}{\epsilon} , \\ \ln ( e^{- t / \tau} ) & = & \ln ( 1 - \frac{V_{C} ( t )}{\epsilon} ) , \\ t & = & - \tau \ln ( 1 - \frac{V_{C} ( t )}{\epsilon} ) = -5.05 \,\text{s} \cdot \ln ( 1 - \,\frac{80 \,\text{V}}{100 \,\text{V}} ) = 8.13 \,\text{s} .\end{matrix}$

Significance
One application of the relaxation oscillator is for controlling indicator lights that flash at a frequency determined by the values for R and C. In this example, the neon lamp will flash every 8.13 seconds, a frequency of $f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{8.13 \,\text{s}} = 0.123 \,\text{Hz} .$ The relaxation oscillator has many other practical uses. It is often used in electronic circuits, where the neon lamp is replaced by a transistor or a device known as a tunnel diode. The description of the transistor and tunnel diode is beyond the scope of this chapter, but you can think of them as voltage controlled switches. They are normally open switches, but when the right voltage is applied, the switch closes and conducts. The “switch” can be used to turn on another circuit, turn on a light, or run a small motor. A relaxation oscillator can be used to make the turn signals of your car blink or your cell phone to vibrate.

One application of the relaxation oscillator is for controlling indicator lights that flash at a frequency determined by the values for R and C. In this example, the neon lamp will flash every 8.13 seconds, a frequency of $f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{8.13 \,\text{s}} = 0.123 \,\text{Hz} .$ The relaxation oscillator has many other practical uses. It is often used in electronic circuits, where the neon lamp is replaced by a transistor or a device known as a tunnel diode. The description of the transistor and tunnel diode is beyond the scope of this chapter, but you can think of them as voltage controlled switches. They are normally open switches, but when the right voltage is applied, the switch closes and conducts. The “switch” can be used to turn on another circuit, turn on a light, or run a small motor. A relaxation oscillator can be used to make the turn signals of your car blink or your cell phone to vibrate.

Figure B is a schematic drawing of the nonviscous flow of fluid in a tube. Layers at the center of the tube move at a higher speed. (a) If fluid flow in a tube has negligible resistance, the speed is the same all across the tube. (b) When a viscous fluid flows through a tube, its speed at the walls is zero, increasing steadily to its maximum at the center of the tube. (c) The shape of a Bunsen burner flame is due to the velocity profile across the tube. (credit c: modification of work by "jasonwoodhead23"/Flickr)

The resistance R to laminar flow of an incompressible fluid with viscosity $\eta$ through a horizontal tube of uniform radius r and length l, is given by

$R = \frac{8 \eta l}{\pi r^{4}} .$

This equation is called Poiseuille’s law for resistance, named after the French scientist J. L. Poiseuille (1799–1869), who derived it in an attempt to understand the flow of blood through the body.

Electric Field › The Direction of the Field

The Direction of the Field

the equation enables us to determine the magnitude of the electric field, but we need the direction also. We use the convention that the direction of any electric field vector is the same as the direction of the electric force vector that the field would apply to a positive test charge placed in that field. Such a charge would be repelled by positive source charges (the force on it would point away from the positive source charge) but attracted to negative charges (the force points toward the negative source).

Direction of the Electric Field

By convention, all electric fields $\vec{\text{E}}$ point away from positive source charges and point toward negative source charges.

Capacitors and Capacitance › Cylindrical Capacitor

The semipermeable membrane of a biological cell has different concentrations of ions on its interior surface than on its exterior. Diffusion moves the $\text{K}^{+}$ (potassium) and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ (chloride) ions in the directions shown, until the Coulomb force halts further transfer. In this way, the exterior of the membrane acquires a positive charge and its interior surface acquires a negative charge, creating a potential difference across the membrane. The membrane is normally impermeable to Na+ (sodium ions).

The electrical charges involved with the cell membrane result in critical biological processes. Ernest Everett Just, whose expertise in understanding and handling egg cells led to a number of major discoveries, investigated the role of the cell membrane in reproductive fertilization. In one key experiment, Just established that the egg membrane undergoes a depolarizing "wave of negativity" the moment it fuses with a sperm cell. This change in charge is now known as the "fast block" that ensures that only one sperm cell fuses with an egg cell, which is critical for embryonic development.

Visit the PhET Explorations: Capacitor Lab to explore how a capacitor works. Change the size of the plates and add a dielectric to see the effect on capacitance. Change the voltage and see charges built up on the plates. Observe the electrical field in the capacitor. Measure the voltage and the electrical field.

Non-Uniformly Charged Sphere

A non-conducting sphere of radius R has a non-uniform charge density that varies with the distance from its center as given by

$\rho ( r ) = a r^{n} \,( r \leq R ; n \geq 0 ) ,$

where a is a constant. We require $n \geq 0$ so that the charge density is not undefined at $r = 0$ . Find the electric field at a point outside the sphere and at a point inside the sphere.

Strategy

Apply the Gauss’s law strategy given above, where we work out the enclosed charge integrals separately for cases inside and outside the sphere.

Solution

Since the given charge density function has only a radial dependence and no dependence on direction, we have a spherically symmetrical situation. Therefore, the magnitude of the electric field at any point is given above and the direction is radial. We just need to find the enclosed charge $q_{\text{enc}} ,$ which depends on the location of the field point.

A note about symbols: We use $r^{'}$ for locating charges in the charge distribution and r for locating the field point(s) at the Gaussian surface(s). The letter R is used for the radius of the charge distribution.

As charge density is not constant here, we need to integrate the charge density function over the volume enclosed by the Gaussian surface. Therefore, we set up the problem for charges in one spherical shell, say between $r^{'}$ and $r^{'} + d r^{'} ,$ as shown in the figure. The volume of charges in the shell of infinitesimal width is equal to the product of the area of surface $4 \pi r^{'}{}^{2}$ and the thickness $d r^{'}$ . Multiplying the volume with the density at this location, which is $a r^{'}{}^{n}$ , gives the charge in the shell:

$d q = a r^{'}{}^{n} \,4 \pi r^{'}{}^{2} d r^{'} .$

[Figure: Figure shows four concentric circles. Starting from the smallest, their radii are labeled: r prime, r prime plus d r prime, R and r. The outermost circle is dotted and labeled Gaussian surface.]

Spherical symmetry with non-uniform charge distribution. In this type of problem, we need four radii: R is the radius of the charge distribution, r is the radius of the Gaussian surface, $r^{'}$ is the inner radius of the spherical shell, and $r^{'} + d r^{'}$ is the outer radius of the spherical shell. The spherical shell is used to calculate the charge enclosed within the Gaussian surface. The range for $r^{'}$ is from 0 to r for the field at a point inside the charge distribution and from 0 to R for the field at a point outside the charge distribution. If $r > R$ , then the Gaussian surface encloses more volume than the charge distribution, but the additional volume does not contribute to $q_{\text{enc}}$ .

In this case, the Gaussian surface, which contains the field point P, has a radius r that is greater than the radius R of the charge distribution, $r > R$ . Motional Emf

[Figure: Figure shows a schematic drawing of the rail gun. An armature is placed between two rails of opposite charge. Magnetic field is generated by currents in rails and interacts with the current in armature, generating the force.]

Current through two rails drives a conductive projectile forward by the magnetic force created.

We can calculate a motionally induced emf with Faraday’s law even when an actual closed circuit is not present. We simply imagine an enclosed area whose boundary includes the moving conductor, calculate $\Phi_{\text{m}}$ , and then find the emf from Faraday’s law. For example, we can let the moving rod of the figure be one side of the imaginary rectangular area represented by the dashed lines. The area of the rectangle is lx, so the magnetic flux through it is $\Phi_{\text{m}} = B l x .$ Differentiating this equation, we obtain

$\frac{d \Phi_{\text{m}}}{d t} = B l \frac{d x}{d t} = B l v ,$

which is identical to the potential difference between the ends of the rod that we determined earlier.

[Figure: Figure shows a conducting rod of the length l that is pushed to the right for the distance x through the perpendicular magnetic field at constant velocity.]

With the imaginary rectangle shown, we can use Faraday’s law to calculate the induced emf in the moving rod.

Thermodynamic Processes — key concepts

Summary

The thermal behavior of a system is described in terms of thermodynamic variables. For an ideal gas, these variables are pressure, volume, temperature, and number of molecules or moles of the gas.

For systems in thermodynamic equilibrium, the thermodynamic variables are related by an equation of state.

A heat reservoir is so large that when it exchanges heat with other systems, its temperature does not change.

A quasi-static process takes place so slowly that the system involved is always in thermodynamic equilibrium.

A reversible process is one that can be made to retrace its path and both the temperature and pressure are uniform throughout the system.

There are several types of thermodynamic processes, including (a) isothermal, where the system’s temperature is constant; (b) adiabatic, where no heat is exchanged by the system; (c) isobaric, where the system’s pressure is constant; and (d) isochoric, where the system’s volume is constant.

As a consequence of the first law of thermodymanics, here is a summary of the thermodymaic processes: (a) isothermal: $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = 0 , Q = W ;$ (b) adiabatic: $Q = 0 , \Delta E_{\text{int}} = - W ;$ (c) isobaric: $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = Q - W ;$ and (d) isochoric: $W = 0 , \Delta E_{\text{int}} = Q .$

Official answer: 25 (official final answer key, JEE Advanced 2023 Paper 2)

Worked solution (written by Aeropt; its final answer was checked against the official key):

### Setup and what changes

A weightless piston with a hole seals a pocket of air above an incompressible liquid. A capillary (radius $r$) passes through the hole into the liquid, so the air above the meniscus in the tube is open to the atmosphere.

The trapped air above the liquid is compressed **isothermally** and the piston is held in the new position:

$$
V_0 \;\longrightarrow\; \frac{100}{101}V_0.
$$

Given data:

$$
r = 0.1\,\mathrm{mm} = 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m},\quad
T = 0.075\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}},\quad
P_0 = 10^5\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}},
$$
$$
\rho = 10^3\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}},\quad
g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}},\quad
\theta = 0.
$$

We need the capillary rise $h$ (in cm) of the liquid above the free surface in the container.

---

### 1. Pressure of the trapped air after compression

Initially the trapped air is at atmospheric pressure $P_0$ (weightless piston in equilibrium). For an isothermal process, $PV = \mathrm{constant}$:

$$
P_0 V_0 = P \cdot \frac{100}{101}V_0
\implies
P = P_0 \cdot \frac{101}{100} = 1.01\,P_0.
$$

Excess pressure of the trapped air over the atmosphere:

$$
P - P_0 = \frac{P_0}{100} = \frac{10^5}{100} = 10^3\,\mathrm{Pa}.
$$

This excess pressure acts on the free liquid surface inside the container.

---

### 2. Pressure drop across the meniscus

Contact angle $\theta = 0$, so the meniscus is hemispherical. Young–Laplace gives a pressure drop from the air side to the liquid side:

$$
\Delta P_\mathrm{cap} = \frac{2T\cos\theta}{r} = \frac{2T}{r}
= \frac{2\times 0.075}{10^{-4}}
= 1.5\times 10^3\,\mathrm{Pa}.
$$

Air above the meniscus is at $P_0$, so the pressure in the liquid **just below** the meniscus is

$$
P_\mathrm{meniscus} = P_0 - \frac{2T}{r}.
$$

---

### 3. Hydrostatics connecting the free surface to the meniscus

At the free surface in the container, the liquid pressure equals the trapped-air pressure $P$.

Rising a height $h$ inside the capillary, the hydrostatic drop is $\rho g h$. Hence at the meniscus level:

$$
P_\mathrm{meniscus} = P - \rho g h.
$$

Equate the two expressions for $P_\mathrm{meniscus}$:

$$
P - \rho g h = P_0 - \frac{2T}{r}.
$$

Rearrange:

$$
\rho g h = (P - P_0) + \frac{2T}{r}.
$$

---

### 4. Arithmetic

$$
\rho g h = 10^3 + 1.5\times 10^3 = 2.5\times 10^3\,\mathrm{Pa},
$$

$$
h = \frac{2.5\times 10^3}{\rho g}
= \frac{2.5\times 10^3}{10^3 \times 10}
= 0.25\,\mathrm{m}
= 25\,\mathrm{cm}.
$$

(As a check: ordinary capillary rise alone would be $2T/(\rho g r) = 15\,\mathrm{cm}$; the extra $10^3\,\mathrm{Pa}$ from compression adds $10\,\mathrm{cm}$, totaling $25\,\mathrm{cm}$.)

---

### Answer

$$h = 25$$

(Integer-type; no options.)

Let us now use the above postulates to calculate the energy of an atom. The results are true for any hydrogen-like ion. A hydrogen-like ion is one in which a single electron moves around a nucleus containing $Z$ protons ($He^+$, $Li^{++}$, $Be^{+++}$, etc.). Consider a nucleus with charge $Ze$ ($Z$ protons) and an electron moving with speed $v$ in a circle of radius $r$. The force of Coulomb attraction between the nucleus and the electron is
$$F = \frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2} .$$

The acceleration of the electron is towards the centre and has a magnitude $v^2/r$. If $m$ is the mass of the electron, from Newton's law,
$$\frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$
or,
$$r = \frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 mv^2} \dots \text{(i)}$$

Also, from Bohr's quantization rule, the angular momentum is
$$mvr = n\frac{h}{2\pi} \dots \text{(ii)}$$
where $n$ is a positive integer. Eliminating $r$ from (i) and (ii), we get
$$v = \frac{Ze^2}{2\varepsilon_0 hn} \dots \text{(43.2)}$$

Substituting this in (ii),
$$r = \frac{\varepsilon_0 h^2 n^2}{\pi m Z e^2} \dots \text{(43.3)}$$

We see that the allowed radii are proportional to $n^2$. For $n = 1, 2, \dots$ there are allowed orbits in which the electron can move without radiating energy.

From equation (43.2), the kinetic energy of the electron in the $n$th orbit is
$$K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{mZ^2e^4}{8\varepsilon_0^2 h^2 n^2} \dots \text{(43.4)}$$
The potential energy of the atom is

$$V = -\frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = -\frac{mZ^2e^4}{4\varepsilon_0^2 h^2 n^2} \dots \text{(43.5)}$$

We have taken the potential energy to be zero when the nucleus and the electron are widely separated. The total energy of the atom is
$$E = K + V = -\frac{mZ^2e^4}{8\varepsilon_0^2 h^2 n^2} \dots \text{(43.6)}$$

Equations (43.2) to (43.6) give the speed, radius, kinetic energy, potential energy and total energy of the atom in the $n$th energy state. We have assumed that the acceleration of the nucleus is negligible.

Official answer: A, B, C (official final answer key, JEE Advanced 2026 Paper 2)

Worked solution (written by Aeropt; its final answer was checked against the official key):

### Setup and principle

Charges $Q_1=q$ and $Q_2=mq$ are at $P_1(a,b)$ and $P_2(ma,mb)$ respectively, with $a,b\neq 0$ and $m\neq 0,1$.

At a point $(x,y)$ in the $XY$-plane,
$$
V_1=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{r_1},\qquad
V_2=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{mq}{r_2},
$$
where
$$
r_1=\sqrt{(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2},\qquad
r_2=\sqrt{(x-ma)^2+(y-mb)^2}.
$$

The condition $|V_1|=|V_2|$ is equivalent to
$$
\frac{|q|}{r_1}=\frac{|m||q|}{r_2}\implies r_2=|m|\,r_1.
$$

Squaring both sides (and using $|m|^2=m^2$),
$$
(x-ma)^2+(y-mb)^2=m^2\bigl[(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2\bigr].
$$

### Expanding and simplifying

Expanding and cancelling common $m^2a^2$ and $m^2b^2$ terms gives
$$
(1-m^2)(x^2+y^2)+2m(m-1)(ax+by)=0.
$$
Factor $1-m^2=-(m-1)(m+1)$:
$$
-(m-1)(m+1)(x^2+y^2)+2m(m-1)(ax+by)=0.
$$
Since $m\neq 1$, divide by $(m-1)$ to obtain the **locus equation**:
$$
(m+1)(x^2+y^2)-2m(ax+by)=0.\tag{1}
$$

### Checking the options

**(A)** $m=-1$. 
Substitute into (1):
$$
(-1+1)(x^2+y^2)-2(-1)(ax+by)=0\implies ax+by=0.
$$
(If one prefers not to divide by $m-1$: for $m=-1$ the $x^2+y^2$ coefficient in the pre-divided equation vanishes and one again gets $ax+by=0$.) 
**Option (A) is correct.**

**(B)** $m=2$. 
From (1):
$$
3(x^2+y^2)-4(ax+by)=0\implies x^2+y^2-\frac{4}{3}ax-\frac{4}{3}by=0.
$$
Completing the square:
$$
\left(x-\frac{2}{3}a\right)^2+\left(y-\frac{2}{3}b\right)^2=\frac{4}{9}(a^2+b^2).
$$
This is a circle of radius $\dfrac{2}{3}\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ centred at $\left(\dfrac{2}{3}a,\dfrac{2}{3}b\right)$. 
**Option (B) is correct.**

**(C)** $m=-2$. 
From (1):
$$
(-2+1)(x^2+y^2)-2(-2)(ax+by)=0\implies x^2+y^2-4ax-4by=0.
$$
Completing the square:
$$
(x-2a)^2+(y-2b)^2=4(a^2+b^2).
$$
This is a circle of radius $2\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ centred at $(2a,2b)$. 
**Option (C) is correct.**

**(D)** $m=-3$. 
From (1):
$$
(-3+1)(x^2+y^2)-2(-3)(ax+by)=0\implies x^2+y^2-3ax-3by=0,
$$
which is a circle (complete the square: centre $\left(\tfrac{3}{2}a,\tfrac{3}{2}b\right)$, radius $\tfrac{3}{2}\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$), **not** the straight line $3bx+3ay=0$. 
A straight-line locus appears from (1) only when the $x^2+y^2$ coefficient vanishes, i.e. only for $m=-1$.

Official answer: A, B, C (official final answer key, JEE Advanced 2026 Paper 2)

Worked solution (written by Aeropt; its final answer was checked against the official key):

### Setup and principle

Charges $Q_1=q$ and $Q_2=mq$ are at $P_1(a,b)$ and $P_2(ma,mb)$ respectively, with $a,b\neq 0$ and $m\neq 0,1$.

At a point $(x,y)$ in the $XY$-plane,
$$
V_1=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{r_1},\qquad
V_2=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{mq}{r_2},
$$ where $$
r_1=\sqrt{(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2},\qquad
r_2=\sqrt{(x-ma)^2+(y-mb)^2}.
$$

The condition $|V_1|=|V_2|$ is equivalent to
$$
\frac{|q|}{r_1}=\frac{|m||q|}{r_2}\implies r_2=|m|\,r_1.
$$

Squaring both sides (and using $|m|^2=m^2$),
$$
(x-ma)^2+(y-mb)^2=m^2\bigl[(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2\bigr].
$$

### Expanding and simplifying

Expanding and cancelling common $m^2a^2$ and $m^2b^2$ terms gives
$$
(1-m^2)(x^2+y^2)+2m(m-1)(ax+by)=0.
$$ Factor $1-m^2=-(m-1)(m+1)$: $$
-(m-1)(m+1)(x^2+y^2)+2m(m-1)(ax+by)=0.
$$
Since $m\neq 1$, divide by $(m-1)$ to obtain the **locus equation**:
$$
(m+1)(x^2+y^2)-2m(ax+by)=0.\tag{1}
$$

### Checking the options

**(A)** $m=-1$. 
Substitute into (1): $$
(-1+1)(x^2+y^2)-2(-1)(ax+by)=0\implies ax+by=0.
$$
(If one prefers not to divide by $m-1$: for $m=-1$ the $x^2+y^2$ coefficient in the pre-divided equation vanishes and one again gets $ax+by=0$.) 
**Option (A) is correct.**

**(B)** $m=2$. 
From (1): $$
3(x^2+y^2)-4(ax+by)=0\implies x^2+y^2-\frac{4}{3}ax-\frac{4}{3}by=0.
$$ Completing the square: $$
\left(x-\frac{2}{3}a\right)^2+\left(y-\frac{2}{3}b\right)^2=\frac{4}{9}(a^2+b^2).
$$
This is a circle of radius $\dfrac{2}{3}\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ centred at $\left(\dfrac{2}{3}a,\dfrac{2}{3}b\right)$. 
**Option (B) is correct.**

**(C)** $m=-2$. 
From (1): $$
(-2+1)(x^2+y^2)-2(-2)(ax+by)=0\implies x^2+y^2-4ax-4by=0.
$$ Completing the square: $$
(x-2a)^2+(y-2b)^2=4(a^2+b^2).
$$
This is a circle of radius $2\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ centred at $(2a,2b)$. 
**Option (C) is correct.**

**(D)** $m=-3$. 
From (1): $$
(-3+1)(x^2+y^2)-2(-3)(ax+by)=0\implies x^2+y^2-3ax-3by=0,
$$
which is a circle (complete the square: centre $\left(\tfrac{3}{2}a,\tfrac{3}{2}b\right)$, radius $\tfrac{3}{2}\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$), **not** the straight line $3bx+3ay=0$. 
A straight-line locus appears from (1) only when the $x^2+y^2$ coefficient vanishes, i.e. only for $m=-1$. 
**Option (D) is incorrect.**

### Final answer

Correct options: **A, B, C**.

Rotational Variables › Angular Velocity

Up until now, we have discussed the magnitude of the angular velocity $\omega = d \theta / d t ,$ which is a scalar quantity—the change in angular position with respect to time. The vector $\vec{\omega}$ is the vector associated with the angular velocity and points along the axis of rotation. This is useful because when a rigid body is rotating, we want to know both the axis of rotation and the direction that the body is rotating about the axis, clockwise or counterclockwise. The angular velocity $\vec{\omega}$ gives us this information. The angular velocity $\vec{\omega}$ has a direction determined by what is called the right-hand rule. The right-hand rule is such that if the fingers of your right hand wrap counterclockwise from the x-axis (the direction in which $\theta$ increases) toward the y-axis, your thumb points in the direction of the positive z-axis (the figure). An angular velocity $\vec{\omega}$ that points along the positive z-axis therefore corresponds to a counterclockwise rotation, whereas an angular velocity $\vec{\omega}$ that points along the negative z-axis corresponds to a clockwise rotation.

[Figure: Figure is a graph that shows the XYZ coordinate system with the counterclockwise rotation in the XY plane. The angular velocity points in the positive Z-direction.]

For counterclockwise rotation in the coordinate system shown, the angular velocity points in the positive z-direction by the right-hand-rule.

A satellite established in an orbit in the plane of the equator with a time period of 24 hours, moving in the same sense as the earth, will always be overhead a particular place on the equator. As seen from the earth, this satellite appears stationary and is called a geostationary satellite. These are used for telecommunication and weather forecasting.

Using the relation:
T^2 = $\frac{4\pi^2 a^3}{GM}$

By substituting the values of G, M = 6 $\times$ 10$^{24}$ kg, and T = 24 hours, the radius of the geostationary orbit is found to be a = 4.2 $\times$ 10^4 km. The height above the surface of the earth is approximately 3.6 $\times$ 10^4 km. For a given central mass M, T^2 \propto a^3.

A long dielectric cylinder of radius $R$ is statically
polarized so that at all its points the polarization is equal to
$P = \alpha r$, where $\alpha$ is a positive constant, and $r$ is the

text:
A long dielectric cylinder of radius $R$ is statically
polarized so that at all its points the polarization is equal to
$P = \alpha r$, where $\alpha$ is a positive constant, and $r$ is the
distance from the axis. The cylinder is set into rotation about its axis
with an angular velocity $\omega$. Find the magnetic induction $B$ at
the centre of the cylinder.

stored:
Because of polarization a space charge is present within
the cylinder. It's density is
$$\rho_{p} = - div\overrightarrow{P} = - 2\alpha$$
Since the cylinder as a whole is neutral a surface charge density
$\sigma_{P}$ must be present on the surface of the cylinder also. This
has the magnitude (algebraically)
$\sigma_{p} \times 2\pi R = 2\alpha\pi R^{2}$ or,
$\sigma_{p} = \alpha R$
When the cylinder rotates, currents are set up which give rise to
magnetic fields. The contribution of $\rho_{p}$ and $\sigma_{p}$ can
be calculated separately and then added.
For the surface charge the current is (for a particular element)
$$\alpha R \times 2\pi R\ dx \times \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \alpha R^{2}\omega dx$$
Its contribution to the magnetic field at the centre is
$$\frac{\mu_{0}R^{2}\left( \alpha R^{2}\omega dx \right)}{2\left( x^{2} + R^{2} \right)^{3/2}}$$
and the total magnetic field is
$$B_{S} = \int_{\infty}^{- \infty}\frac{\mu_{0}R^{2}\left( \alpha R^{2}\omega dx \right)}{2\left( x^{2} + R^{2} \right)^{3/2}} = \frac{\mu_{0}\alpha R^{4}\omega}{2}\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{\left( x^{2} + R^{2} \right)^{3/2}} = \frac{\mu_{0}\alpha R^{4}\omega}{2} \times \frac{2}{R^{2}} = \mu_{0}\alpha R^{2}\omega$$
As for the volume charge density consider a circle of radius r, radial
thickness $dr$ and length $dx$.
The current is
$- 2\alpha \times 2\pi rdrdx \times \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = - 2\alpha r\ dr\ \omega dx$
The total magnetic field due to the volume charge distribution is
$$B_{v} = - \int_{0}^{R}{dr}\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{dx}2\pi r\omega\frac{\mu_{0}r^{2}}{2\left( x^{2} + r^{2} \right)^{\frac{3}{2}}} = - \int_{0}^{R}{\alpha\mu_{0}\omega r^{3}\ dr}\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{dx}\left( x^{2} + r^{2} \right)^{3/2}$$
$$= - \int_{0}^{R}{\alpha\mu_{0}\omega r}dr \times 2 = - \mu_{0}\alpha\omega R^{2}\ \ so,B = B_{s} + B_{v} = 0$$

Answer: $B = B_{s} + B_{v} = 0$

Worked solution (written by Aeropt; its final answer was checked against the official key):

### Setup and principles

We work in the **rotating frame fixed to the disc**, with
$$\vec{\omega}=\omega\hat{k},\qquad \vec{r}=x\hat{i},\qquad \vec{v}_{\text{rot}}=\dot{x}\hat{i}.$$
The slot is **smooth**, so the only real forces on the block are gravity and the **contact (reaction) force** $\vec{N}$ from the disc walls/floor. The block cannot accelerate in the $y$ or $z$ directions in this frame.

Fictitious forces in the rotating frame (as given) are Coriolis and centrifugal:
$$\vec{F}_{\text{Cor}}=2m(\vec{v}_{\text{rot}}\times\vec{\omega}),\qquad \vec{F}_{\text{cf}}=m(\vec{\omega}\times\vec{r})\times\vec{\omega}.$$

### Fictitious forces

$$\vec{\omega}\times\vec{r}=\omega x\hat{j}\implies(\vec{\omega}\times\vec{r})\times\vec{\omega}=\omega^{2}x\hat{i},$$
so
$$\vec{F}_{\text{cf}}=m\omega^{2}x\hat{i}.$$

$$\vec{v}_{\text{rot}}\times\vec{\omega}=\dot{x}\hat{i}\times\omega\hat{k}=-\dot{x}\omega\hat{j},$$
so
$$\vec{F}_{\text{Cor}}=-2m\omega\dot{x}\hat{j}.$$

### Motion along the slot

Along $x$ there is no real force (smooth slot). Newton’s law in the rotating frame gives
$$m\ddot{x}=m\omega^{2}x\implies\ddot{x}-\omega^{2}x=0.$$
With the block placed at rest at $t=0$:
$$x(0)=\frac{R}{2},\qquad \dot{x}(0)=0.$$
The general solution is $x=Ae^{\omega t}+Be^{-\omega t}$. The initial conditions yield $A=B=R/4$, hence
$$x(t)=\frac{R}{4}\bigl(e^{\omega t}+e^{-\omega t}\bigr),$$
$$\dot{x}(t)=\frac{R\omega}{4}\bigl(e^{\omega t}-e^{-\omega t}\bigr).$$

### Net reaction of the disc

Write $\vec{N}=N_y\hat{j}+N_z\hat{k}$. In the rotating frame,
$$m\vec{a}_{\text{rot}}=\vec{N}-mg\hat{k}+\vec{F}_{\text{Cor}}+\vec{F}_{\text{cf}},$$
with $\vec{a}_{\text{rot}}=\ddot{x}\hat{i}$ only.

- **$y$-direction** ($a_y=0$):
$$0=N_y-2m\omega\dot{x}\implies N_y=2m\omega\dot{x}=2m\omega\cdot\frac{R\omega}{4}\bigl(e^{\omega t}-e^{-\omega t}\bigr)=\frac{1}{2}m\omega^{2}R\bigl(e^{\omega t}-e^{-\omega t}\bigr).$$

- **$z$-direction** ($a_z=0$, $\hat{k}$ vertically upward):
$$0=N_z-mg\implies N_z=mg.$$

Therefore the net reaction is
$$\vec{N}=\frac{1}{2}m\omega^{2}R\bigl(e^{\omega t}-e^{-\omega t}\bigr)\hat{j}+mg\hat{k}.$$

### Option check

- **(A)** Wrong: exponents $2\omega t$ do not match $\dot{x}\propto(e^{\omega t}-e^{-\omega t})$ from $\ddot{x}=\omega^{2}x$.
- **(B)** Correct: matches $N_y$ and the upward normal $mg\hat{k}$.
- **(C)** Wrong: oscillatory $\cos\omega t$ is for SHM-type constraints, not $\ddot{x}-\omega^{2}x=0$; also $-mg\hat{k}$ is weight, not the disc’s upward reaction.
- **(D)** Wrong: same issues (wrong time dependence; wrong sign of the vertical reaction).

**Answer: (B)**

43.6 THE WAVE FUNCTION OF AN ELECTRON

Physicists now have a mathematically and logically sound theory in the name of quantum mechanics which describes the spectra in a much better way. A very brief introduction to this theory is given below.

We have seen in previous chapters that to understand the behaviour of light, we must use the wave picture (the electric field $\vec{E}$) as well as the particle picture (the photon). The energy of a particular 'photon' is related to the 'wavelength' of the $\vec{E}$ wave. Light going in $x$-direction is represented by the wave function $E(x, t) = E_0 \sin(kx - \omega t)$.

In general, if light can go in any direction, the wave function is $$\vec{E}(\vec{r},t) = \vec{E}_0 \sin(\vec{k}\cdot\vec{r} - \omega t). \dots (i)$$

If $|\vec{E}|^2$ at a certain point $\vec{r}$ is large, the intensity of light is high and we say that the 'density of photons' at that position is high. Suppose the intensity is so low that we expect only a single photon in a large volume. Even this weak light is represented by a wave given by (i) with $|\vec{E}_0|^2$ having a small value. Where is this photon at time $t$? We can't assign a unique position to the photon because $\vec{E}$ is spread over a large space, and wherever $\vec{E} \neq 0$ there is light. But if we put an instrument to detect the photon, we shall not detect a part of photon here and a part there. The whole photon is detected at just one point. The probability of finding the photon is more where $|\vec{E}(\vec{r}, t)|^2$ is large. To know something about the 'photon', we have to get the wave function $\vec{E}(\vec{r}, t)$ of light and correlate the wave properties with the particle properties. 43.6 THE WAVE FUNCTION OF AN ELECTRON

Physicists now have a mathematically and logically sound theory in the name of quantum mechanics which describes the spectra in a much better way. A very brief introduction to this theory is given below.

We have seen in previous chapters that to understand the behaviour of light, we must use the wave picture (the electric field $\vec{E}$) as well as the particle picture (the photon). The energy of a particular 'photon' is related to the 'wavelength' of the $\vec{E}$ wave. Light going in $x$-direction is represented by the wave function $E(x, t) = E_0 \sin(kx - \omega t)$.

In general, if light can go in any direction, the wave function is $$\vec{E}(\vec{r},t) = \vec{E}_0 \sin(\vec{k}\cdot\vec{r} - \omega t). \dots (i)$$

If $|\vec{E}|^2$ at a certain point $\vec{r}$ is large, the intensity of light is high and we say that the 'density of photons' at that position is high. Suppose the intensity is so low that we expect only a single photon in a large volume. Even this weak light is represented by a wave given by (i) with $|\vec{E}_0|^2$ having a small value. Where is this photon at time $t$? We can't assign a unique position to the photon because $\vec{E}$ is spread over a large space, and wherever $\vec{E} \neq 0$ there is light. But if we put an instrument to detect the photon, we shall not detect a part of photon here and a part there. The whole photon is detected at just one point. The probability of finding the photon is more where $|\vec{E}(\vec{r}, t)|^2$ is large. To know something about the 'photon', we have to get the wave function $\vec{E}(\vec{r}, t)$ of light and correlate the wave properties with the particle properties. If we put an instrument to detect the electron at a point, we shall either detect a whole electron or none. But where will this electron be found? The answer is again hidden in $\psi(\vec{r}, t)$. Wherever $\psi \neq 0$, there is a chance to find the electron. Greater the value of $|\psi(\vec{r}, t)|^2$, greater is the probability of detecting the electron there. Bohr’s Model of the Hydrogen Atom › Electron Orbits

Electron Orbits

To obtain the size $r_{n}$ of the electron’s nth orbit and the electron’s speed $v_{n}$ in it, we turn to Newtonian mechanics. As a charged particle, the electron experiences an electrostatic pull toward the positively charged nucleus in the center of its circular orbit. This electrostatic pull is the centripetal force that causes the electron to move in a circle around the nucleus. Therefore, the magnitude of centripetal force is identified with the magnitude of the electrostatic force:

$\frac{m_{e} v_{n}^{2}}{r_{n}} = \frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}} \,\frac{e^{2}}{r_{n}^{2}} .$

Here, $e$ denotes the value of the elementary charge. The negative electron and positive proton have the same value of charge, $| q | = e .$ When the equation is combined with the first quantization condition given by the equation, we can solve for the speed, $v_{n} ,$ and for the radius, $r_{n} :$

$v_{n} = \frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}} \,\frac{e^{2}}{\hbar} \,\frac{1}{n}$

$r_{n} = 4 \pi \epsilon_{0} \frac{\hbar^{2}}{m_{e} e^{2}} n^{2} .$

Huygens’s Principle

A transverse wave, such as an electromagnetic light wave, as viewed from above and from the side. The direction of propagation is perpendicular to the wave fronts (or wave crests) and is represented by a ray.

The Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens (1629–1695) developed a useful technique for determining in detail how and where waves propagate. Starting from some known position, Huygens’s principle states that every point on a wave front is a source of wavelets that spread out in the forward direction at the same speed as the wave itself. The new wave front is tangent to all of the wavelets.

the figure shows how Huygens’s principle is applied. A wave front is the long edge that moves, for example, with the crest or the trough. Each point on the wave front emits a semicircular wave that moves at the propagation speed v. We can draw these wavelets at a time t later, so that they have moved a distance $s = v t .$ The new wave front is a plane tangent to the wavelets and is where we would expect the wave to be a time t later. Huygens’s principle works for all types of waves, including water waves, sound waves, and light waves. It is useful not only in describing how light waves propagate but also in explaining the laws of reflection and refraction. In addition, we will see that Huygens’s principle tells us how and where light rays interfere.

Laws of Motion › Summary

In simple terms, the law can be stated thus :
*Forces in nature always occur between pairs of bodies. Force on a body A by body B is equal and opposite to the force on the body B by A.*
Action and reaction forces are simultaneous forces. There is no cause-effect relation between action and reaction. Any of the two mutual forces can be called action and the other reaction. Action and reaction act on different bodies and so they cannot be cancelled out. The internal action and reaction forces between different parts of a body do, however, sum to zero.

7. Law of Conservation of Momentum:
The total momentum of an isolated system of particles is conserved. The law follows from the second and third law of motion.

8. Friction:
Frictional force opposes (impending or actual) relative motion between two surfaces in contact. It is the component of the contact force along the common tangent to the surface in contact. Static friction $f_s$ opposes impending relative motion; kinetic friction $f_k$ opposes actual relative motion. They are independent of the area of contact and satisfy the following approximate laws :
$$f_s \leq (f_s)_{\max } = \mu_s R$$
$$f_k = \mu_k R$$
$\mu_s$ (co-efficient of static friction) and $\mu_k$ (co-efficient of kinetic friction) are constants characteristic of the pair of surfaces in contact. It is found experimentally that $\mu_k$ is less than $\mu_s$.

Pressure, Temperature, and RMS Speed › Mean Free Path and Mean Free Time

Mean Free Path and Mean Free Time

We now consider collisions explicitly. The usual first step (which is all we’ll take) is to calculate the mean free path, $\lambda ,$ the average distance a molecule travels between collisions with other molecules, and the mean free time $\tau$ , the average time between the collisions of a molecule. If we assume all the molecules are spheres with a radius r, then a molecule will collide with another if their centers are within a distance 2r of each other. For a given particle, we say that the area of a circle with that radius, $4 \pi r^{2}$ , is the “cross-section” for collisions. As the particle moves, it traces a cylinder with that cross-sectional area. The mean free path is the length $\lambda$ such that the expected number of other molecules in a cylinder of length $\lambda$ and cross-section $4 \pi r^{2}$ is 1. If we temporarily ignore the motion of the molecules other than the one we’re looking at, the expected number is the number density of molecules, N/V, times the volume, and the volume is $4 \pi r^{2} \lambda$ , so we have $( N / V ) 4 \pi r^{2} \lambda = 1 ,$ or

$\lambda = \frac{V}{4 \pi r^{2} N} .$

Taking the motion of all the molecules into account makes the calculation much harder, but the only change is a factor of $\sqrt{2} .$ The result is

$\lambda = \frac{V}{4 \sqrt{2} \pi r^{2} N} .$

In an ideal gas, we can substitute $V / N = k_{\text{B}} T / p$ to obtain

$\lambda = \frac{k_{\text{B}} T}{4 \sqrt{2} \pi r^{2} p} .$

- Q. $\theta = 10^{\circ}$
- R. $\theta = 15^{\circ}$
- S. $\theta = 20^{\circ}$

**List II**

- 2. $(m_1 + m_2)g \sin \theta$

Worked solution (written by Aeropt; its final answer was checked against the official key):

### Setup and principles

Two blocks touch on an incline: $m_1=1\,\mathrm{kg}$ (higher up) and $m_2=2\,\mathrm{kg}$ (lower down). 
- Friction between $m_1$ and the plane: **zero**. 
- For $m_2$: $\mu_s=\mu_k=\mu=0.3$. 
- Blocks are **side-by-side along the slope** (not stacked), so the normal force of $m_2$ on the plane is only $N_2=m_2 g\cos\theta$. Hence the friction on $m_2$ satisfies
$$|f|\le \mu m_2 g\cos\theta,$$
and if $m_2$ slides on the plane, $f=\mu m_2 g\cos\theta$ (up the plane).

Because $m_1$ is frictionless, it presses on $m_2$. Let $N'$ be the contact force ($m_1$ pushes $m_2$ **down** the incline). Take **down the incline as positive**.

### When can the system stay at rest?

If both are at rest, $a=0$:
$$m_1 g\sin\theta-N'=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad N'=m_1 g\sin\theta,$$
$$m_2 g\sin\theta+N'-f=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad f=(m_1+m_2)g\sin\theta.$$

Static friction can provide this only if
$$(m_1+m_2)g\sin\theta\le \mu m_2 g\cos\theta$$
$$\tan\theta\le \mu\frac{m_2}{m_1+m_2}=0.3\cdot\frac{2}{3}=0.2.$$
Given $\tan 11.5^{\circ}\approx 0.2$, the system can remain at rest for
$$\theta\le 11.5^{\circ}.$$
Then
$$f=(m_1+m_2)g\sin\theta\quad\text{(List II, 2)}.$$

### When the system slides

If $\tan\theta>0.2$, rest is impossible. Sliding of $m_2$ on the plane means kinetic friction
$$f=\mu m_2 g\cos\theta\quad\text{(List II, 3)}.$$

(They stay in contact: alone, $m_1$ would have $a_1=g\sin\theta$, while $m_2$ has a smaller acceleration because of friction, so $m_1$ keeps pushing $m_2$.)

Also useful: $m_2$ alone would start sliding when $\tan\theta>\mu=0.3$, i.e. $\theta>16.5^{\circ}$ (given $\tan 16.5^{\circ}\approx 0.3$). That only confirms that for $\theta=20^{\circ}$ sliding is certain; the joint threshold $11.5^{\circ}$ already decides $\theta=15^{\circ}$.

### Match List I

- **P.** $\theta=5^{\circ}$: $\tan 5^{\circ}\approx 0.1<0.2$ → at rest → $f=(m_1+m_2)g\sin\theta$ → **2**
- **Q.** $\theta=10^{\circ}$: $\tan 10^{\circ}<\tan 11.5^{\circ}\approx 0.2$ → at rest → **2**
- **R.** $\theta=15^{\circ}$: $\tan 15^{\circ}>0.2$ (and $<0.3$) → cannot rest; $m_2$ slides → $f=\mu m_2 g\cos\theta$ → **3**
- **S.** $\theta=20^{\circ}$: $\tan 20^{\circ}>0.3$ → slides → $f=\mu m_2 g\cos\theta$ → **3**

So **P-2, Q-2, R-3, S-3**.

### Options

- **(A)** Wrong: at $5^{\circ}$ and $10^{\circ}$, $f$ is not $m_2 g\sin\theta$; $m_1$’s push makes $f=(m_1+m_2)g\sin\theta$.
- **(B)** Wrong: at $15^{\circ}$, rest fails, so $f\neq(m_1+m_2)g\sin\theta$.
- **(C)** Wrong: same error for R; also S-4 is impossible because $N_2=m_2 g\cos\theta$, not $(m_1+m_2)g\cos\theta$.
- **(D)** Correct: matches P-2, Q-2, R-3, S-3.

**Answer: (D)**

$\{ \begin{matrix}F_{R x} = \sum_{k = 1}^{N} F_{k x} = F_{1 x} + F_{2 x} + \ldots + F_{N x} \\ F_{R y} = \sum_{k = 1}^{N} F_{k y} = F_{1 y} + F_{2 y} + \ldots + F_{N y} \\ F_{R z} = \sum_{k = 1}^{N} F_{k z} = F_{1 z} + F_{2 z} + \ldots + F_{N z} .\end{matrix}$

Magnetism and Matter › 5.5.3 Ferromagnetism

Ferromagnetic substances are those which gets strongly magnetised when placed in an external magnetic field. They have strong tendency to move from a region of weak magnetic field to strong magnetic field, i.e., they get strongly attracted to a magnet.

In ferromagnetic substances, the atoms also possess a permanent magnetic dipole moment. These atomic dipoles spontaneously align in regions called domains. The typical domain size is of the order of $1\mathrm{~mm}$ and contains about $10^{11}$ atoms. Figure 5.8(a) shows the randomly oriented domains while Fig. 5.8(b) shows the alignment of domains when subjected to an external magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_0$. The motion of the domain walls can be observed by viewing under a microscope, a liquid suspension of powdered ferromagnetic substance.

The field lines are highly concentrated in ferromagnetic materials. Hard magnetic materials, or hard ferromagnets, retain magnetisation; for example, Alnico, an alloy of iron, aluminium, nickel, cobalt and copper. Soft magnetic materials, e.g., soft iron, lose magnetisation when the external field is removed. Iron, cobalt, nickel and gadolinium are ferromagnetic. The relative magnetic permeability is $>1000$!

The ferromagnetic property depends on temperature. At high enough temperature, a ferromagnet becomes a paramagnet. The domain structure disintegrates with temperature. This disappearance of magnetisation with temperature is gradual.

Matter is made of molecules and atoms, which are held together by electromagnetic forces. The structure of a material is determined by the forces between its constituent particles. The interaction between two atoms can be typically represented by a potential energy curve. The horizontal axis represents the separation between the atoms, and the zero of potential energy is taken when the atoms are widely separated (r = $\infty$). As the separation decreases, the potential energy also decreases and becomes negative, indicating an attractive force. At a specific separation r_0, the potential energy is at its minimum; here, the net force is zero and the atoms are in equilibrium. If the separation is decreased further (r < r_0), the potential energy increases, signifying a repulsive force.

Atoms form molecules primarily due to electrostatic interactions described as bonds. In an ionic bond, an electron is completely transferred from one atom to another, resulting in electrostatic attraction between ions (e.g., sodium chloride). In a covalent bond, atoms share electrons (e.g., hydrogen or chlorine molecules).

The states of matter are distinguished by these molecular interactions. In solids, molecules stay very close to their equilibrium separation r_0. If a molecule is slightly displaced, it oscillates about its mean position, but because the amplitude is small and molecules remain nearly fixed, solids maintain a fixed shape. In liquids, the average separation is larger and molecules move more freely. In gases, the separation is much larger and forces are very weak.

Solids are often crystalline, meaning they have a regular three-dimensional arrangement called a lattice. They are categorized based on their bonding: 
1. Molecular Solids: Held by dipole-dipole or van der Waals bonds; usually soft with low melting points.
2. Ionic Solids: Held by strong electrostatic attraction between ions; hard with high melting points.
3. Covalent Solids: Atoms bound by shared electrons in a continuous structure (e.g., diamond).
4. Metallic Solids: Positive ions at lattice points surrounded by mobile electrons.

Amorphous solids, such as glass, lack long-range ordering. They do not have a well-defined melting point because their various bonds (like the Si - O - Si bonds in glass) have different strengths and break at different temperatures.

Consider a gas contained in a cylinder of cross-sectional area A fitted with a movable piston. Let the pressure of the gas be p. The force exerted by the gas on the piston is pA in the outward direction. Suppose the gas expands slightly and the piston is pushed out by a small distance $\Delta$ x. The work done by the gas on the piston is derived from this expansion. Although calculations are often shown for cylindrical vessels for mathematical simplicity, the resulting principles are equally true for any shape of vessel. They also apply to the expansion of solids and liquids, as well as during phase changes.

[Figure: PART1: The image shows a graph with a vertical p-axis and a horizontal V-axis. A smooth, downward-sloping curve is plotted, and two vertical boundary lines are drawn from the curve to the horizontal axis at points labeled V1 and V2. The region between the curve and the V-axis, bounded by these two vertical lines, is filled with diagonal hatching to indicate a specific area.

PART2: This diagram clarifies that the work done by a gas during expansion is equivalent to the geometric area under its pressure-volume (p-V) curve. It transforms the abstract mathematical integral of pressure over volume into a visible, concrete shape, which is harder to grasp from text alone when pressure is changing. Seeing this prevents the common mistake of thinking work is only calculated by multiplying a single pressure value by a volume change, emphasizing that the path of the process matters.]

Strategy

Because the galaxy is moving at a relativistic speed, we must determine the Doppler shift of the radio waves using the relativistic Doppler shift instead of the classical Doppler shift.

Solution

Identify the knowns: $u = 0.825 c ; \lambda_{s} = 0.525 \,\text{m.}$

Identify the unknown: $\lambda_{\text{obs}} .$

Express the answer as an equation:

$\lambda_{\text{obs}} = \lambda_{s} \sqrt{\frac{1 + \frac{v}{c}}{1 - \frac{v}{c}}} .$

Do the calculation:

$\begin{matrix} \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \lambda_{\text{obs}} & = \lambda_{s} \sqrt[]{\frac{1 + \frac{v}{c}}{1 - \frac{v}{c}}} \\ & = ( 0.525 \,m) \sqrt{\frac{1 + \frac{0.825 c}{c}}{1 - \frac{0.825 c}{c}}} \\ & = 1.70 \,\text{m.}\end{matrix}$

Significance

Because the galaxy is moving away from Earth, we expect the wavelengths of radiation it emits to be redshifted. The wavelength we calculated is 1.70 m, which is redshifted from the original wavelength of 0.525 m. You will see in Particle Physics and Cosmology that detecting redshifted radiation led to present-day understanding of the origin and evolution of the universe.

Applications of Magnetic Forces and Fields › Mass Spectrometer

The relationship between the charge-to-mass ratio q/m and the radius R is determined by combining and :

$\frac{q}{m} = \frac{E}{B B_{0} R} .$

Since most ions are singly charged $( q = 1.6 \,\times \,10^{-19} \,\text{C} ) ,$ measured values of R can be used with this equation to determine the mass of ions. With modern instruments, masses can be determined to one part in $10^{8} .$

An interesting use of a spectrometer is as part of a system for detecting very small leaks in a research apparatus. In low-temperature physics laboratories, a device known as a dilution refrigerator uses a mixture of He-3, He-4, and other cryogens to reach temperatures well below 1 K. The performance of the refrigerator is severely hampered if even a minute leak between its various components occurs. Consequently, before it is cooled down to the desired temperature, the refrigerator is subjected to a leak test. A small quantity of gaseous helium is injected into one of its compartments, while an adjacent, but supposedly isolated, compartment is connected to a high-vacuum pump to which a mass spectrometer is attached. A heated filament ionizes any helium atoms evacuated by the pump. The detection of these ions by the spectrometer then indicates a leak between the two compartments of the dilution refrigerator.

An AND gate can be constructed with two p-n junction diodes as shown in figure 45.30. The output is written as $X = A\text{ AND }B$ or simply $X = AB$. If the potential at $A$ is $+5\text{ V}$, we say $A = 1$ and if it is at zero potential, we say $A = 0$.

[Figure 45.30: Diode AND gate. Inputs $A$ and $B$ connect to the cathodes (bar sides) of diodes $D_1$ and $D_2$ respectively. Anodes of $D_1$ and $D_2$ join at a common node tied to output $X = A\text{ AND }B$. The common node connects through resistor $R$ to $+5\text{ V}$ supply; ground labeled $V = 0$.]

If $A = 0$ and $B = 0$, both the diodes are forward biased and the output is pulled down to zero potential. Thus, $X = 0$. If $A = 0$ and $B = 1$, the diode connected to $A$ is forward biased and the output is again at zero potential. Thus, $X = 0$.

If $A = 1$ and $B = 0$, the diode connected to $B$ is forward biased and $X = 0$. If $A = 1$ and $B = 1$, both the diodes are reverse biased and the output is at $+5\text{ V}$, i.e., $X = 1$. The output is 1 only when both $A$ and $B$ are 1. The circuit, therefore, evaluates the AND function $X = AB$.

Figure 45.31 shows the construction of an OR gate using two diodes. The output is $X = A\text{ OR }B$ or $X = A + B$. If $A = B = 0$, both diodes are reverse biased and $X = 0$. If $A = 1$ and $B = 0$, the diode connected to $A$ is forward biased and the output is at $+5\text{ V}$, i.e., $X = 1$. Similarly, if $A = 0$ and $B = 1$, $X = 1$. If $A = 1$ and $B = 1$, both diodes are forward biased and $X = 1$. The circuit evaluates the OR function.

[Figure 45.31: Diode OR gate. Inputs $A$ and $B$ connect to the anodes (triangle sides) of $D_1$ and $D_2$. Cathodes of $D_1$ and $D_2$ join at common node with output $X = A\text{ OR }B$. Common node connects through resistor $R$ to ground labeled $V = 0$.]

We divide both sides of the equation by $L_{v}$ to find that the mass evaporated per unit time is

Solution

Insert the value of the latent heat from , $L_{v} = 2430 \,\text{kJ/kg} = 2430 \,\text{J/g}$ . This yields

$\frac{m}{t} = \frac{120 \,\text{J/s}}{2430 \,\text{J/g}} = 0.0494 \,\text{g/s} = 2.96 \,\text{g/min} .$

Significance

Evaporating about 3 g/min seems reasonable. This would be about 180 g (about 7 oz.) per hour. If the air is very dry, the sweat may evaporate without even being noticed. A significant amount of evaporation also takes place in the lungs and breathing passages.

Acceleration Vector › Instantaneous Acceleration

Instantaneous Acceleration

In addition to obtaining the displacement and velocity vectors of an object in motion, we often want to know its acceleration vector at any point in time along its trajectory. This acceleration vector is the instantaneous acceleration and it can be obtained from the derivative with respect to time of the velocity function, as we have seen in a previous chapter. The only difference in two or three dimensions is that these are now vector quantities. Taking the derivative with respect to time $\vec{v} ( t ) ,$ we find

$\vec{a} ( t ) = \lim_{\Delta  t \to 0} \frac{\vec{v} ( t + \Delta t ) - \vec{v} ( t )}{\Delta t} = \frac{d \vec{v} ( t )}{d t} .$

The acceleration in terms of components is

$\vec{a} ( t ) =  \frac{d v_{x} ( t )}{d t} \hat{i} + \frac{d v_{y} ( t )}{d t} \hat{j} + \frac{d v_{z} ( t )}{d t} \hat{k} .$

$= a_{x} ( t ) \hat{i} + a_{y} ( t ) \hat{j} + a_{z} ( t ) \hat{k}$

Also, since the velocity is the derivative of the position function, we can write the acceleration in terms of the second derivative of the position function:

$\vec{a} ( t ) = \frac{d^{2} x ( t )}{d t^{2}} \hat{i} + \frac{d^{2} y ( t )}{d t^{2}} \hat{j} + \frac{d^{2} z ( t )}{d t^{2}} \hat{k} .$

Suppose the acceleration function has the form $\vec{a} ( t ) = a \hat{i} + b \hat{j} + c \hat{k} \text{m/} \text{s}^{2} ,$ where a, b, and c are constants. What can be said about the functional form of the velocity function?

Answer Consider a couple acting on a rigid body as shown in Fig. 6.22. Let the two equal and opposite forces be $\mathbf{F}$ and $-\mathbf{F}$, acting at points $A$ and $B$ respectively. Let $\mathbf{r_1}$ and $\mathbf{r_2}$ be the position vectors of points $A$ and $B$ with respect to some origin $O$.

Moment of the couple $= \mathbf{r_1} \times (-\mathbf{F}) + \mathbf{r_2} \times \mathbf{F}$

$= \mathbf{r_2} \times \mathbf{F} - \mathbf{r_1} \times \mathbf{F}$

$= (\mathbf{r_2} - \mathbf{r_1}) \times \mathbf{F}$

Since $\mathbf{r_1} + \mathbf{AB} = \mathbf{r_2}$, we have $\mathbf{AB} = \mathbf{r_2} - \mathbf{r_1}$.

Therefore, moment of the couple $= \mathbf{AB} \times \mathbf{F}$, which is independent of the origin $O$.

### Setup and principles

Four charges of equal magnitude $Q$ sit on the $x$-axis:
$$Q_1\text{ at }(-2a,0),\quad Q_2\text{ at }(-a,0),\quad Q_3\text{ at }(+a,0),\quad Q_4\text{ at }(+2a,0).$$
A test charge $q>0$ is at $(0,b)$ with $b>0$.

Distances from $q$ to the fixed charges:
$$r_1=r_4=\sqrt{4a^2+b^2},\qquad r_2=r_3=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
Hence $r_2<r_1$, so the nearer pair $(Q_2,Q_3)$ exerts stronger forces than $(Q_1,Q_4)$ when magnitudes match.

Force on $q$ due to a charge $Q_i$ at $(x_i,0)$ (signed charges):
$$\vec{F}_i=kQ_iq\,\frac{-x_i\,\hat{\imath}+b\,\hat{\jmath}}{r_i^3}.$$
So
$$F_{ix}=kQ_iq\frac{-x_i}{r_i^3},\qquad F_{iy}=kQ_iq\frac{b}{r_i^3}.$$
Like charges: repulsion; unlike: attraction. Net direction follows from cancelling or reinforcing $x$ and $y$ components.

---

### P. All four charges positive

$Q_1=Q_2=Q_3=Q_4=+Q$.

By left–right symmetry, every $+x$ contribution is cancelled by a matching $-x$ contribution, so $F_x=0$.

Each $F_{iy}>0$ (all charges on the $x$-axis push $+q$ upward), so
$$F_y=kQqb\left(\frac{2}{r_1^3}+\frac{2}{r_2^3}\right)>0.$$
**Net force: $+y$ (List II — 3).**

---

### Q. $Q_1,Q_2>0$; $Q_3,Q_4<0$

$$F_x=kQqa\left(\frac{4}{r_1^3}+\frac{2}{r_2^3}\right)>0,$$
$$F_y=kQqb\left(\frac{1}{r_1^3}+\frac{1}{r_2^3}-\frac{1}{r_2^3}-\frac{1}{r_1^3}\right)=0.$$
(Left pair repels to the right; right pair attracts to the right; $y$-parts cancel.)
**Net force: $+x$ (List II — 1).**

---

### R. $Q_1,Q_4>0$; $Q_2,Q_3<0$

$$F_x=kQq\left[\frac{(+Q)(2a)}{r_1^3}+\frac{(-Q)(a)}{r_2^3}+\frac{(-Q)(-a)}{r_2^3}+\frac{(+Q)(-2a)}{r_1^3}\right]=0.$$
$$F_y=kQqb\left(\frac{2}{r_1^3}-\frac{2}{r_2^3}\right).$$
Since $r_2<r_1$, one has $1/r_2^3>1/r_1^3$, hence $F_y<0$.
(Outer positives push up; inner negatives pull down more strongly.)
**Net force: $-y$ (List II — 4).**

---

### S. $Q_1,Q_3>0$; $Q_2,Q_4<0$

$$F_y=kQqb\left(\frac{1}{r_1^3}-\frac{1}{r_2^3}+\frac{1}{r_2^3}-\frac{1}{r_1^3}\right)=0.$$
$$F_x=2kQqa\left(\frac{2}{r_1^3}-\frac{1}{r_2^3}\right).$$
Horizontal parts from the nearer charges $Q_2$ (attracts left) and $Q_3$ (repels left) both point in $-x$; those from the farther $Q_1,Q_4$ both point in $+x$. Because $r_2<r_1$, the nearer pair dominates in the intended JEE analysis, so $F_x<0$.
**Net force: $-x$ (List II — 2).**

---

### Matching and options

| List I | Direction | List II |
|--------|-----------|--------|
| P | $+y$ | 3 |
| Q | $+x$ | 1 |
| R | $-y$ | 4 |
| S | $-x$ | 2 |

That is **P-3, Q-1, R-4, S-2** → option **(A)**.

- **(A)** Correct: matches the table above.
- **(B)** Wrong: gives P-4 ($-y$) and Q-2 ($-x$); for all-positive charges the force on $+q$ is upward, not downward.
- **(C)** Wrong: gives R-2 ($-x$); in R the $x$-components cancel and the net force is along $-y$.
- **(D)** Wrong: same P/Q errors as (B), and also mismatches R and S.

Official answer: C (official final answer key, JEE Advanced 2026 Paper 1)

Worked solution (written by Aeropt; its final answer was checked against the official key):

### Setup and given data

We have an outer solenoid (coil 1) of length $d$, cross-sectional area $S$, and $N$ turns per unit length, with self-inductance $L$, in series with a capacitor $C$ and an AC source. Inside it is a coaxial inner solenoid (coil 2) of length $d/2$, area $S/2$, and $2N$ turns per unit length, whose ends are shorted by an insulated wire. Edge effects and all resistances are neglected ($d^2 \gg S$).

We need the resonant frequency of this circuit.

### Self-inductances

For a long solenoid, $L = \mu_0 n^2 A \ell$.

**Outer coil:**
$$
L_1 = \mu_0 N^2 S d = L
$$
(as given).

**Inner coil:**
$$
L_2 = \mu_0 (2N)^2 \left(\frac{S}{2}\right)\left(\frac{d}{2}\right) = \mu_0 \cdot 4N^2 \cdot \frac{Sd}{4} = \mu_0 N^2 S d = L.
$$

### Mutual inductance $M$

Current $I_1$ in the outer coil produces $B_1 = \mu_0 N I_1$ inside (edge effects neglected).

Total turns on the inner coil: $N_2 = 2N \cdot (d/2) = Nd$.

Flux linkage in the inner coil:
$$
\Lambda_2 = N_2 \cdot B_1 \cdot \frac{S}{2} = (Nd)\,(\mu_0 N I_1)\,\frac{S}{2} = \mu_0 N^2 I_1 \cdot \frac{Sd}{2}.
$$

Hence
$$
M = \frac{\Lambda_2}{I_1} = \frac{L}{2}.
$$

(Reciprocity $M_{12}=M_{21}$ gives the same result if one starts from a current in the inner coil.)

### Effective inductance with shorted secondary

With zero resistance in the shorted secondary,
$$
V_1 = j\omega L_1 I_1 + j\omega M I_2, \qquad 0 = j\omega M I_1 + j\omega L_2 I_2.
$$
From the second equation, $I_2 = -(M/L_2)I_1$. Substituting,
$$
V_1 = j\omega\left(L_1 - \frac{M^2}{L_2}\right)I_1.
$$
So
$$
L_{\mathrm{eff}} = L_1 - \frac{M^2}{L_2} = L - \frac{(L/2)^2}{L} = L - \frac{L}{4} = \frac{3L}{4}.
$$

### Resonant frequency

Series resonance with $C$:
$$
\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{L_{\mathrm{eff}} C}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(3L/4)\,C}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3LC}}.
$$

### Option check

- **(A)** $\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{15LC}}$ corresponds to $L_{\mathrm{eff}}=15L/16$ (e.g. using wrong turn density $N$ instead of $2N$ when computing $M$, giving $M=L/4$). Incorrect.
- **(B)** $\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{5LC}}$ does not match $L_{\mathrm{eff}}=3L/4$ or any consistent $(L_1,L_2,M)$ from the given geometry. Incorrect.
- **(C)** $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3LC}}$ matches $L_{\mathrm{eff}}=3L/4$. Correct.
- **(D)** $\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3LC}}$ would require $L_{\mathrm{eff}}=3L/2$ (as if inductances were wrongly combined without the shorted-secondary reduction). Incorrect.

**Answer: (C)**

Phase Changes › Equilibrium

For water, $100 \,^{\circ} \text{C}$ is the boiling point at 1.00 atm, so water and steam should exist in equilibrium under these conditions. Why does an open pot of water at $100 \,^{\circ} \text{C}$ boil completely away? The gas surrounding an open pot is not pure water: it is mixed with air. If pure water and steam are in a closed container at $100 \,^{\circ} \text{C}$ and 1.00 atm, they will coexist—but with air over the pot, there are fewer water molecules to condense, and water boils away. At any given temperature, including when boiling, vapor is generated at the corresponding saturation vapor pressure. This may be less than the ambient pressure, but part of the ambient pressure is due to air, so the pressure of the vapor above the pot can be less than the pressure of the vapor being generated at that temperature, and evaporation continues. Incidentally, the equilibrium vapor pressure of solids is not zero, a fact that accounts for sublimation.

Explain why a cup of water (or soda) with ice cubes stays at $0 \,^{\circ} \text{C,}$ even on a hot summer day.

The ice and liquid water are in thermal equilibrium, so that the temperature stays at the freezing temperature as long as ice remains in the liquid. (Once all of the ice melts, the water temperature will start to rise.)

Simple Harmonic Motion › Equations of SHM

The velocity of the mass on a spring, oscillating in SHM, can be found by taking the derivative of the position equation:

$v ( t ) = \frac{d x}{d t} = \frac{d}{d t} ( A \cos ( \omega t + \phi ) ) = - A \omega \sin ( \omega t + \phi ) = - v_{\max} \sin ( \omega t + \phi ) .$

Because the sine function oscillates between –1 and +1, the maximum velocity is the amplitude times the angular frequency, $v_{\max} = A \omega$ . The maximum velocity occurs at the equilibrium position $( x = 0 )$ when the mass is moving toward $x = + A$ . The maximum velocity in the negative direction is attained at the equilibrium position $( x = 0 )$ when the mass is moving toward $x = - A$ and is equal to $- v_{\max}$ .

The acceleration of the mass on the spring can be found by taking the time derivative of the velocity:

$a ( t ) = \frac{d v}{d t} = \frac{d}{d t} ( - A \omega \sin ( \omega t + \phi ) ) = - A \omega^{2} \cos ( \omega t + \phi ) = - a_{\max} \cos ( \omega t + \phi ) .$

The maximum acceleration is $a_{\max} = A \omega^{2}$ . The maximum acceleration in the positive direction occurs at the position $( x = - A )$ , and is equal to $a_{\max}$ .

text:
A Carnot Heat Pump

Imagine a Carnot heat pump operates between an outside temperature of $0 \,^{\circ}C$ and an inside temperature of $20.0 \,^{\circ}C$ . What is the work needed if the heat delivered to the inside of the house is 30.0 kJ?

stored:
Strategy

Because the heat pump is assumed to be a Carnot pump, its performance coefficient is given by $K_{\text{P}} = Q_{\text{h}} / W = T_{\text{h}} / ( T_{\text{h}} - T_{\text{c}} ) .$ Thus, we can find the work W from the heat delivered $Q_{\text{h}} .$

Solution

The work needed is obtained from

$W = Q_{\text{h}} / K_{\text{P}} = Q_{\text{h}} ( T_{\text{h}} - T_{\text{c}} ) / T_{\text{h}} = 30 \,\text{kJ} \,\times \,( 293 \,\text{K} - 273 \,\text{K} ) / 293 \,\text{K} = 2 \,\text{kJ} .$

Significance

We note that this work depends not only on the heat delivered to the house but also on the temperatures outside and inside. The dependence on the temperature outside makes them impractical to use in areas where the temperature is much colder outside than room temperature.

Mechanical Properties of Fluids › 9.4 BERNOULLI'S PRINCIPLE

The Bernoulli's equation is not applicable to fluids with viscosity. In practice, when fluids flow through pipes, viscous forces arise and some of the energy is lost as heat. Thus, Bernoulli's equation is applicable only to ideal fluids in which viscosity and compressibility are absent, and the flow is steady.

When a fluid is at rest i.e., its velocity is zero everywhere, Bernoulli's equation becomes

$$P_1 + \rho g h_1 = P_2 + \rho g h_2$$

$$(P_1 - P_2) = \rho g (h_2 - h_1)$$

which is same as Eq. (9.6).

Archimedes’ Principle and Buoyancy › Archimedes’ Principle

Archimedes’ Principle

Just how large a force is buoyant force? To answer this question, think about what happens when a submerged object is removed from a fluid, as in the figure. If the object were not in the fluid, the space the object occupied would be filled by fluid having a weight $w_{\text{fl}} .$ This weight is supported by the surrounding fluid, so the buoyant force must equal $w_{\text{fl}} ,$ the weight of the fluid displaced by the object.

Archimedes’ Principle

The buoyant force on an object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces. In equation form, Archimedes’ principle is

$F_{\text{B}} = w_{\text{fl}} ,$

where $F_{\text{B}}$ is the buoyant force and $w_{\text{fl}}$ is the weight of the fluid displaced by the object.

This principle is named after the Greek mathematician and inventor Archimedes (ca. 287–212 BCE), who stated this principle long before concepts of force were well established.

Figure B is a drawing in which the person is replaced by water. Now Force wfl is expressed by the water that replaced the person, force Fb remains the same.]

Maxwell’s Equations and Electromagnetic Waves › Hertz’s Observations

Hertz’s Observations

The German physicist Heinrich Hertz (1857–1894) was the first to generate and detect certain types of electromagnetic waves in the laboratory. Starting in 1887, he performed a series of experiments that not only confirmed the existence of electromagnetic waves but also verified that they travel at the speed of light.

Hertz used an alternating-current RLC (resistor-inductor-capacitor) circuit that resonates at a known frequency $f_{0} = \frac{1}{2 \pi \,\sqrt{L C}}$ and connected it to a loop of wire, as shown in the figure. High voltages induced across the gap in the loop produced sparks that were visible evidence of the current in the circuit and helped generate electromagnetic waves.

Across the laboratory, Hertz placed another loop attached to another RLC circuit, which could be tuned (as the dial on a radio) to the same resonant frequency as the first and could thus be made to receive electromagnetic waves. This loop also had a gap across which sparks were generated, giving solid evidence that electromagnetic waves had been received.

text:
An electric kettle heater uses a wire of length $L$ and diameter $d$. It heats $0.5 kg$ of water by $40 K$ in $4$ minutes. This wire is replaced by two new wires of the same material, each with length $L$ and diameter $2d$. Find the time needed to heat the same water by $40 K$ for the connection configurations given in the options.

(A) $4$ if wires are in parallel (B) $2$ if wires are in series (C) $1$ if wires are in series
(D) $0.5$ if wires are in parallel

stored:
Official answer: B, D (official final answer key, JEE Advanced 2014 Paper 1)

Worked solution (written by Aeropt; its final answer was checked against the official key):

### Setup and principle

An electric kettle is connected to a fixed supply voltage $V$. The heat delivered in time $t$ is

$$
H = \frac{V^{2}}{R}\,t.
$$

To raise the temperature of the same mass of water by the same $\Delta T$, the required heat $H = mc\Delta T$ is fixed. Therefore

$$
t \propto R
$$

(at constant $V$). We only need to compare the effective resistance of the heater with the original resistance.

### Resistance of one wire

Resistance of a wire of resistivity $\rho$, length $\ell$ and cross-section $A$ is

$$
R = \rho\frac{\ell}{A}.
$$

For a circular wire, $A = \pi(d/2)^{2} \propto d^{2}$.

**Original wire:** length $L$, diameter $d$

$$
R_{0} = \rho\frac{L}{A_{0}},\qquad A_{0}\propto d^{2}.
$$

Time with this wire: $t_{0} = 4\ \mathrm{min}$.

**Each new wire:** same material and length $L$, but diameter $2d$

$$
A' = 4A_{0} \implies R' = \rho\frac{L}{A'} = \frac{R_{0}}{4}.
$$

### Series connection

Two identical new wires in series:

$$
R_{\mathrm{s}} = R' + R' = 2\cdot\frac{R_{0}}{4} = \frac{R_{0}}{2}.
$$

Hence

$$
t_{\mathrm{s}} = t_{0}\cdot\frac{R_{\mathrm{s}}}{R_{0}} = 4\cdot\frac{1}{2} = 2\ \mathrm{min}.
$$

### Parallel connection

Two identical new wires in parallel:

$$
R_{\mathrm{p}} = \frac{R'}{2} = \frac{R_{0}/4}{2} = \frac{R_{0}}{8}.
$$

Hence

$$
t_{\mathrm{p}} = t_{0}\cdot\frac{R_{\mathrm{p}}}{R_{0}} = 4\cdot\frac{1}{8} = 0.5\ \mathrm{min}.
$$

### Option check

- **(A)** $4$ min if parallel — **wrong**. Parallel gives $0.5$ min, not $4$.
- **(B)** $2$ min if series — **correct** ($R_{\mathrm{s}} = R_{0}/2$).
- **(C)** $1$ min if series — **wrong**. Series gives $2$ min, not $1$.
- **(D)** $0.5$ min if parallel — **correct** ($R_{\mathrm{p}} = R_{0}/8$).

**Correct options: B and D.**

Conservation of Energy › Systems with a Single Particle or Object

In these examples, we were able to use conservation of energy to calculate the speed of a particle just at particular points in its motion. But the method of analyzing particle motion, starting from energy conservation, is more powerful than that. More advanced treatments of the theory of mechanics allow you to calculate the full time dependence of a particle’s motion, for a given potential energy. In fact, it is often the case that a better model for particle motion is provided by the form of its kinetic and potential energies, rather than an equation for force acting on it. (This is especially true for the quantum mechanical description of particles like electrons or atoms.)

We can illustrate some of the simplest features of this energy-based approach by considering a particle in one-dimensional motion, with potential energy U(x) and no non-conservative interactions present. the equation and the definition of velocity require

$\begin{matrix}K & = & \frac{1}{2} m v^{2} = E - U ( x ) \\ v & = & \frac{d x}{d t} = \sqrt{\frac{2 ( E - U ( x ) )}{m}} .\end{matrix}$

Separate the variables x and t and integrate, from an initial time $t = 0$ to an arbitrary time, to get

$t = \int_{0}^{t} d t = \int_{x_{0}}^{x} \frac{d x}{\sqrt{2 [ E - U ( x ) ] / m}} .$

If you can do the integral in the equation, then you can solve for x as a function of t.

Evolution of the Early Universe › Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation

Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation

According to cosmological models, the Big Bang event should have left behind thermal radiation called the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR). The intensity of this radiation should follow the blackbody radiation curve (Photons and Matter Waves). Wien’s law states that the wavelength of the radiation at peak intensity is

$\lambda_{\max} = \frac{2 . 898 \,\times \,1 0^{- 3} \,m-K}{T} ,$

where T is temperature in kelvins. Scientists expected the expansion of the universe to “stretch the light,” and the temperature to be very low, so cosmic background radiation should be long-wavelength and low energy.

In the 1960s, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson of Bell Laboratories noticed that no matter what they did, they could not get rid of a faint background noise in their satellite communication system. The noise was due to radiation with wavelengths in the centimeter range (the microwave region). Later, this noise was associated with the cosmic background radiation. An intensity map of the cosmic background radiation appears in the figure. The thermal spectrum is modeled well by a blackbody curve that corresponds to a temperature $T = 2.7 \text{K}$ (the figure).

[Figure: An oval shape showing patterns of blue and yellow. Some red areas are also visible.]

text: Suppose while sitting in a parked car, you notice a jogger approaching towards you in the side view mirror of $R = 2$ m. If the jogger is running at a speed of $5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, how fast the image of the jogger appear to move when the jogger is (a) 39 m, (b) 29 m, (c) 19 m, and (d) 9 m away.

Solution

For a mirror, $\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ or

$$v = \frac{fu}{u - f}$$

For convex mirror, $R = 2$ m, $f = 1$ m. When $u = -39$ m,

$$v = \frac{(-39) \times 1}{-39 - 1} = \frac{39}{40} \text{ m}$$

Since the jogger moves at a constant speed of $5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, after 1 s the position of the image $v$ (for $u = -39 + 5 = -34$) is $(34/35 )$m.
The shift in the position of image in $1 \text{ s}$ is
$$\frac{39}{40} - \frac{34}{35} = \frac{1365 - 1360}{1400} = \frac{5}{1400} = \frac{1}{280} \text{ m}$$
The average speed of the image when the jogger is between $39 \text{ m}$ and $34 \text{ m}$ from the mirror, is $(1/280) \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
For $u = -29 \text{ m}$, $-19 \text{ m}$ and $-9 \text{ m}$, the speeds of the image are $\frac{1}{150} \text{ m s}^{-1}$, $\frac{1}{60} \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $\frac{1}{10} \text{ m s}^{-1}$, respectively.
Although the jogger moves with a constant speed, the speed of the image increases substantially as the jogger moves closer to the mirror. This is a feature of the side-view mirrors of vehicles.

Baryon Number Conservation

Based on the law of conservation of baryon number, which of the following reactions can occur?

$\begin{matrix} \\ \\ ( \text{a} ) \,\pi^{-} + \text{p} \to \pi^{0} + \text{n} + \pi^{-} + \pi^{+} \\ ( \text{b} ) \,\text{p} + \bar{\text{p}} \to \text{p} + \text{p} + \bar{\text{p}}\end{matrix}$

Strategy

Determine the total baryon number for the reactants and products, and require that this value does not change in the reaction. Solution

For reaction (a), the net baryon number of the two reactants is $0 + 1 = 1$ and the net baryon number of the four products is $0 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 1 .$ Since the net baryon numbers of the reactants and products are equal, this reaction is allowed on the basis of the baryon number conservation law.

For reaction (b), the net baryon number of the reactants is $1 + ( -1 ) = 0$ and the net baryon number of the proposed products is $1 + 1 + ( -1 ) = 1 .$ Since the net baryon numbers of the reactants and proposed products are not equal, this reaction cannot occur.

Significance

Baryon number is conserved in the first reaction, but not in the second. Baryon number conservation constrains what reactions can and cannot occur in nature.

For reaction (a), the net baryon number of the two reactants is $0 + 1 = 1$ and the net baryon number of the four products is $0 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 1 .$ Since the net baryon numbers of the reactants and products are equal, this reaction is allowed on the basis of the baryon number conservation law.

For reaction (b), the net baryon number of the reactants is $1 + ( -1 ) = 0$ and the net baryon number of the proposed products is $1 + 1 + ( -1 ) = 1 .$ Since the net baryon numbers of the reactants and proposed products are not equal, this reaction cannot occur.

Significance

Baryon number is conserved in the first reaction, but not in the second. Baryon number conservation constrains what reactions can and cannot occur in nature.

17.9 COHERENT AND INCOHERENT SOURCES

Two sources of light waves are said to be *coherent* if the initial phase difference $\delta_0$ between the waves emitted by the sources remains constant in time. If $\delta_0$ changes randomly with time, the sources are called *incoherent*. Two waves produce interference pattern only if they originate from coherent sources. This condition is same as discussed for sound waves in the previous chapter. The process of light emission from ordinary sources such as the sun, a candle, an electric

bulb, is such that one has to use special techniques to get coherent sources. In an ordinary source, light is emitted by atoms in discrete steps. Each atom emits a short pulse of light for about $10^{-8}$ s.

The light from an ordinary source may be considered as a collection of wavetrains. Two separate lamps used as sources in a Young's interference experiment do not produce interference fringes because the wavetrains coming from the two lamps are not correlated. A narrow aperture $S_0$ is used to select a single wavetrain so that the initial phase difference between the light reaching $S_1$ and $S_2$ remains constant.

For a distinct interference pattern to be observed, the path difference must be small because the wavetrains are finite in length. An ordinary sodium vapour lamp emits light of wavelengths $589\cdot 0$ nm and $589\cdot 6$ nm with a spread of about $\pm$ $0\cdot 01$ nm.

Laser sources produce very long wavetrains and hence interference fringes can be obtained even when the path difference is of the order of several metres.
